core_claim: Circadian rhythms (≈24-hour oscillations) are entrained by environmental light; the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) synchronizes neuroendocrine, metabolic, and behavioral rhythms. Architectural light exposure affects melatonin, cortisol, alertness, and sleep architecture.

falsification_criteria: Morning bright light exposure does not phase-advance circadian rhythm or increase alertness compared to control
Evening light exposure (blue-spectrum) does not suppress melatonin or delay sleep onset
Chronic circadian misalignment (due to shift work, poor light exposure) does not degrade sleep quality or health outcomes
scope_boundaries: Applies to nearly all organisms (cyanobacteria to humans); mechanisms vary
Does NOT fully explain acute sleep needs (sleep homeostasis is separate, though linked)
Individual differences (chronotype, age, light sensitivity) are substantial; generalizations are population-level

environmental_predictions.statement: Workplaces/homes with morning bright light exposure (≥1,000 lux, especially 460-490nm wavelength) show earlier circadian phase, improved sleep timing, higher daytime alertness, and lower evening melatonin compared to dim/evening-only light
environmental_predictions.mechanism: ipRGC (intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells) detect 460-490nm light and signal to SCN. Morning light advances circadian phase; evening avoidance prevents phase delay.

competing_predictions.prediction: Alertness benefits are due to acute norepinephrine/dopamine response, not circadian phase shift

environmental_predictions.statement: Environments with evening blue light (screens, bright artificial light) suppress melatonin and delay sleep onset by 30-60 minutes; effect is dose-dependent (brightness) and timing-dependent (closer to sleep, larger effect)
environmental_predictions.mechanism: Blue light activates ipRGCs; evening ipRGC signaling inhibits melatonin synthesis in pineal gland, delaying sleep onset and shortening total sleep.

environmental_predictions.statement: Chronic circadian misalignment (e.g., night shift work or low daytime light exposure) produces sustained melatonin disruption, shortened/fragmented sleep, and long-term health risk (metabolic, cancer, cardiovascular)
environmental_predictions.mechanism: Misalignment prevents proper SCN entrainment. Melatonin rhythm decouples from sleep-wake cycle. Chronic desynchrony degrades multiple physiological systems (glucose homeostasis, immune function, tumor suppression).

competing_predictions.prediction: Sleep disruption is felt as body budget dysregulation, not driven by circadian mechanisms

characteristic_questions: What is the light exposure profile of this environment (timing, intensity, spectrum)?
Is there morning bright light (≥1,000 lux, optimal 460-490nm) to entrain circadian rhythm?
What evening light exposure occurs (blue-enriched screens, artificial lighting)?
Does the environment support consistent sleep-wake timing, or demand shift-work schedules?
Are there windows for natural light access, or is the space artificially lit?

panel_persona.voice: I evaluate environments through the lens of circadian entrainment: Does the light exposure pattern align with human biology, or does it create misalignment? What are the consequences for sleep, alertness, and health?
typical_critiques: Light intensity, spectrum (wavelength), timing, and duration all matter; specify all four in predictions.
Melatonin suppression does NOT always produce insomnia; effects are real but variable.
Circadian misalignment is a major health risk, but causality is sometimes hard to disentangle from sleep loss itself.
Individual chronotypes vary; morning light benefits evening-chronotype people but may disrupt morning-chronotype people.
blind_spots: Tendency to treat light exposure as the only circadian input; food timing, social cues, and activity also entrain
May underestimate role of sleep homeostasis (separately from circadian timing)
Limited account of how aging changes light sensitivity and circadian timing
Does not explain why some people adjust to shift work better than others (neuroticism, personality)
complementary_frameworks: interoceptive-construction (sleep quality is constructed from body state and arousal prediction)
default-mode-dynamics (circadian timing modulates DMN-TPN switching; sleep deprivation impairs TPN)
neuromodulatory-systems (melatonin is neuromodulator; cortisol rhythm reflects HPA circadian output)

meta.notes: Circadian biology is robustly confirmed across species. Light effects on melatonin and sleep are well-established. Growing evidence for health consequences of misalignment (shift-work disease).
